bib.title: Future of Work with AI Agents: Auditing Automation and Augmentation Potential across the U.S. Workforce

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Future of Work with AI Agents: Auditing Automation and Augmentation Potential across the U.S. Workforce", Yijia Shao*, Humishka Zope*, Yucheng Jiang, Jiaxin Pei, David Nguyen, Erik Brynjolfsson, Diyi Yang (Stanford). arXiv:2506.06576v3, 1 Feb 2026 (listed as cs.CY; no venue printed, treat as preprint). 2025/2026.

COVERAGE: 129,424 of 129,424 chars read, 45 of 45 pages (main text, limitations, appendices A-F, tables). Skimmed: reference list (~chars 58k-62k), the large Table 1 mixed-effects coefficient dump, and the transcript examples in F.2 (read the opening of each, not every transcript). Appendix C.2-C.4 and D (demographics) only partly read; I did not extract their numbers.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- The HAS is a 5-level scale from H1 (no human involvement) to H5 (human involvement essential); H1-H2 favour automation, H3-H5 augmentation. It is positioned as complementing SAE L0-L5, which is "AI-first".
  number: 5 levels
  setup: worker and expert Likert rating of "how much collaboration between you and the AI system would be needed", per O*NET task
  quote: "H1: AI agent handles the task entirely on its own. H2: AI agent needs minimal human input for optimal performance. H3: AI agent and human form equal partnership, outperforming either alone. H4: AI agent requires human input to successfully complete the task. H5: AI agent cannot function without continuous human involvement."
  where: p.4, chars ~4,300-5,000. Also: "Unlike SAE driving automation levels (Committee et al., 2014) that adopt an “AI-first” perspective, HAS provides a human-centered lens" and "higher HAS levels are not inherently better—different levels suit different AI roles."
- Workers want more human agency than experts say is technically needed.
  number: 26.9% matching; 47.5% in lower triangle
  setup: 844 tasks, majority vote of workers vs. at least two AI experts per task
  quote: "Among 844 tasks, 26.9% receive matching levels from workers and AI experts. Figure 6a shows workers generally prefer higher levels of human agency than what experts deem technologically necessary, with 47.5% of tasks fall into the lower triangle of the matrix."
  where: p.11, ~char 36,800
- H3 (equal partnership) is the most common dominant worker-desired level.
  number: 45.2% of occupations (47 of 104); H2 35.6%, H4 16.3%, H1 1.9%, H5 1.0%
  setup: 104 occupations, dominant worker-desired level per occupation
  quote: "H3 emerges as the dominant worker-desired level in 47 out of 104 occupations analyzed." Intro: "45.2% of occupations have H3 (equal partnership) as the dominant worker-desired level"
  where: p.3 and p.12. The percentages come from the Fig 6b labels in the extraction (H1: 1.9%, H2: 35.6%, H3: 45.2%, H4: 16.3%, H5: 1.0%).
- Experts rate few occupations as needing essential human involvement. Many sit at H1.
  number: 16 of 104 occupations predominantly H1 (expert view); H5 only for Mathematicians and Aerospace Engineers; workers: only Editors
  setup: expert-assessed feasible level, early-2025 capability
  quote: "According to AI experts’ ratings, 16 out of 104 occupations are predominantly H1, even based on current capability estimates."
  where: p.13
- Where worker and expert HAS views diverge most (largest Jensen-Shannon divergence), experts are usually at H1 and workers at H2 or H4.
  number: top JSD 0.830 (Power Distributors and Dispatchers, workers H4, experts H3); Medical Transcriptionists 0.675 (H2 vs H1); Financial Examiners 0.569 (H4 vs H1); Travel Agents 0.571 (H2 vs H1); Lawyers 0.525 (H3 vs H2)
  setup: per-occupation JSD between task-level distributions of worker-desired and expert-feasible HAS
  quote: "Disagreements are most pronounced in the lower HAS range as Table 7 shows that five of the ten occupations with the highest JSD scores are also those that experts rate as H1 dominant."
  where: p.11, Table 7 (Appendix E.5)
- H5 tasks are marked by interpersonal communication (workers) and by interpersonal communication plus domain expertise (experts).
  number: none
  quote: "worker ratings highlight Interpersonal Communication as a defining feature of H5 tasks (Figure 6c), while expert ratings emphasize both Interpersonal Communication and Domain Expertise (Figure 6d)."
  where: p.13
- Routine, easily verified tasks tend to need lower human agency.
  number: none
  quote: "those involving more routine tasks and easily verifiable outcomes tend to require lower human agency."
  where: p.13
- Workers want automation for a minority of tasks, mainly to free time.
  number: 46.1% of tasks with mean desire >3; 69.38% cite freeing time; 46.6% repetitive; 25.5% stressful
  setup: 844 tasks, 104 occupations, 1,500 workers, Jan-May 2025
  quote: "for 46.1% of tasks, workers currently performing them express a positive attitude (i.e., Aw(t)>3) toward AI agent automation, even after explicitly considering concerns such as job loss and reduced enjoyment"
  where: p.9. Note the reasons are for ratings with A_w >= 3, N=3,618. The text says "46.6%" for both repetitiveness and quality; the Fig 4b counts are 605/573/508 for repetitive (by sector), so treat 46.6% with care.
- Desire-capability mismatch (Red Light zone and others): the four zones are Green Light (high desire, high capability), Red Light (high capability, low desire), R&D Opportunity (high desire, low capability), Low Priority.
  number: 41.0% of Y Combinator company-task mappings fall in Low Priority plus Red Light; desire vs capability Spearman rho = 0.17
  setup: YC companies (cut-off 28 Apr 2025) mapped to tasks by gpt-4.1-mini; expert capability vs worker desire
  quote: "41.0% of YC companies are mapped to Low Priority and Automation “Red Light” Zone; while many promising tasks within the “Green Light” Zone and Opportunity Zone remain under-addressed by current investments." and "no strong correlation between Aw(t) and Ae(t) (Spearman ρ= 0.17, p <1e−6)"
  where: p.10-11
- Zone shares in the full dataset (from the robustness appendix): Green Light 43.13%, Red Light 31.64%, Low Priority 12.56%, R&D Opportunity 12.68%.
  quote: "41.60% of tasks fall in the Automation “Green Light” Zone (vs. 43.13% in the full dataset), 31.09% in the Automation “Red Light” Zone (vs. 31.64%), 15.13% in the Low Priority zone (vs. 12.56%), and 12.18% in the R&D Opportunity zone (vs. 12.68%)."
  where: Appendix B.2, ~char 80,000
- Usage data lags worker desire.
  number: 1.26%
  quote: "the top 10 occupations with the highest average automation desire account for only 1.26% of total usage."
  setup: Claude.ai usage Dec 2024-Jan 2025 (Handa et al. 2025)
  where: p.9
- Workers resist where they enjoy the task or fear job loss. Concerns are mostly about trust.
  number: enjoyment rho = -0.28; job loss concern rho = -0.22; 28.0% voiced fears; of those, 45.0% accuracy/trust, 23.0% job replacement, 16.3% lack of human qualities; Arts, Design and Media 17.1% of tasks with positive desire
  quote: "28.0% expressed fears, concerns, or negative sentiment ... (1) lack of trust in AI systems’ accuracy, capability, or reliability (45.0%), (2) fear of job replacement (23.0%), and (3) the absence of human qualities or capabilities in AI (16.3%)."
  where: p.9-10, Table 9
- Collaboration paradigms workers describe (LLM topic modelling of audio transcripts, Claude 3 Opus with LLooM).
  number: role-based 23.1%, assistantship 23.0%, pure automation 16.5%, separation of tasks between AI and humans 12.0%
  quote: "Role-based support 23.1% Assistantship 23.0% Automation 16.5% Separation of Tasks between AI and Humans 12.0%"
  where: Table 10, p.45
- Skills shift: info-processing skills (analysing data, updating knowledge) rank high on wage but lower on required human agency. Interpersonal and organisational skills rank higher on required human agency than on wage.
  number: none (rank comparison only)
  setup: O*NET Generalized Work Activities; wage from BLS May 2024; agency from expert H_e
  quote: "from information processing toward interpersonal and organizational competencies."
  where: Fig 7, p.14-15

LIMITS
- Authors concede: O*NET tasks omit new tasks that agents create. Workers may not know agent capabilities. Workers may withhold honest answers out of job-security or surveillance fears. Only 104 of 287 computer-using occupations are covered. Data is a snapshot of early 2025 (Jan-May) and will shift with capability.
- Expert agreement is moderate: Krippendorff alpha 0.539 (capability) and 0.511 (feasible HAS). Each task had at least two experts, with SD <= 1.
- Task-level signal in worker desire is weak: ICC = 0.050 overall. It is 0.405 on a 238-task "high-signal" subset, where the zone shares stay stable.
- Scope: computer-compatible tasks done at least monthly (2,131 tasks, 287 occupations filtered with gpt-4o). Physical work is excluded. Agents are defined as digital only.
- HAS is a self-reported preference or expert judgement per task. It does not measure actual agent autonomy or oversight behaviour. It is not a runtime autonomy ladder like SAE levels, and the paper never ties H1-H5 to loop designs, approval gates or measured oversight cost.
- Workers rate HAS conditional on "if AI were to assist", so it mixes preference with perceived need. The paper's own caveat is that higher levels are not better.
- The YC and arXiv mappings use gpt-4.1-mini (LLM-labelled). The YC counts show no significant difference across zones in Fig 5b.
- Sample: 1,678 recruited, 7,016 task ratings, 1,500 kept after requiring at least 10 per occupation. Recruitment through Prolific, Upwork and LinkedIn.

BUILDS ON: SAE L0-L5 driving automation (Committee et al., 2014); Autor 2015 (automation vs augmentation); Brynjolfsson 2022 (Turing trap); Autor, Levy, Murnane 2003 (skill content); Eloundou et al. 2023 (LLM exposure); Handa et al. 2025 (Claude.ai usage); Shao et al. 2024b (Collaborative Gym, human-agent collaboration); Armstrong et al. 2024 and Gödöllei and Beck 2023 (worker views on automation); Parasuraman 2000, Frank et al. 2019, Shah and White 2024 (task characteristics); Lam et al. 2024 (LLooM). Agent definition draws on Castelfranchi 1994, Russell and Norvig 1995, Wooldridge and Jennings 1995.

CODE: none.

FIGURES (I did not run the captions script; these are from the extracted text)
- Fig 2 (p.5): the H1-H5 definitions with team dynamics and example tasks, e.g. H1 "Transcribe data to worksheets", "Run monthly network reports". Best for the note's ladder table.
- Fig 5 (p.10): desire-capability landscape with four zones, plus YC and arXiv counts per zone.
- Fig 6 (p.12): worker-desired vs expert-feasible HAS matrix, dominant-level distribution, task characteristics radar.
- Fig 10 and Table 7 (p.34-35): per-occupation HAS distributions and top-10 JSD.

PROBLEMS: Extraction is clean text. Figure labels and axis values are interleaved, so the zone and YC numbers in Fig 5 are not reliably tied to their zones in the extraction (for example the 134.35/117.63/... values). I did not use those. Some typos exist in the text (the "46.6%" repeated for two reasons). The page numbers above are approximate, derived from the printed page headers. The extraction was saved at /tmp/shao.txt. No embedded instructions were found in the PDF. A caution for the target note: the paper's HAS describes preferred human involvement per task. It is not an autonomy level for agent loops, so mapping it onto an autonomy ladder is the caller's interpretation, not the paper's claim.
